generatedProse.concept-context: Psychology gives you material of very different shapes, and the three families fit different shapes. A model with linked components, such as a model of memory or an information-processing account, suits a visual mind map that shows how the parts connect. A set of key terms, effect names or definitions suits flashcards or reading aloud. A research procedure or experimental design, which is a sequence of steps, suits a kinaesthetic walk-through. Choosing well means looking at the material first.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students revise the same module, which has three very different topics: a multi-part model of memory, a list of key terms and effects, and the procedure of a classic experiment.

Tom likes flashcards, so he makes flashcards for all three. The terms suit cards well. But the model of memory becomes a pile of cards in no order, and the links between its components are lost. The experiment's procedure, which only makes sense as a sequence, does not fit cards at all. The technique was fine; using the same one for everything was not.

Amara looks at each topic first. The key terms and effects become flashcards. The model of memory becomes a mind map that lays out the components and shows how they feed into each other. The experiment's procedure becomes a physical walk-through, stepping through each stage in order. Each technique was chosen to fit what the topic is.

Both students revised all three topics. Only Amara matched the technique to the material rather than forcing one method onto everything.
generatedProse.summary: Active techniques fall into three families: visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. In psychology, a linked model suits a visual map, a set of terms suits flashcards or reading aloud, and a research procedure suits a kinaesthetic walk-through. None is better than the others; the skill is matching the technique to the material. You can now describe the families, place a technique in its family, and choose techniques that fit what you are revising.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Amara use a mind map for the memory model and flashcards for the key terms?

items.text: She matched each technique to the kind of material, rather than using one method for everything.
She preferred variety and wanted her revision to feel less boring.
She had run out of flashcards and had to improvise.
Mind maps are always better than flashcards in psychology.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara chose each technique to fit the kind of material, which is selecting to fit.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the reason that is about matching the method to the material.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara matched each technique to the kind of material, rather than forcing one method onto everything. It was not about variety, chance or one technique being best.
